options.name: Point-to-point integration with network-trusted internal edges
options.summary: Services integrate directly. External edges are authenticated; internal edges are trusted because they sit inside the network boundary. Contracts are documented per interface without central governance.
checklist: interface inventory complete for internal and external edges
trust boundary marked on each edge - the marking is what reveals the assumption
transport and payload protection stated per interface
error, retry and poison-message handling defined per async path
which interfaces differ between Prod and RTL (stubs, mocks, sandboxes) recorded

questions.question: For each edge crossing a trust boundary, is authorisation verified at the edge, or inferred from the caller's network location?
Which integrations are stubbed in RTL, and does the stub hide a failure mode that Prod will exhibit?
How many point-to-point edges will exist at the end state, and is that number maintainable?

anchors.metric: Request rate per interface at peak
Interfaces stubbed or mocked in RTL

risks.statement: Internal edges trusted by network location mean any workload that reaches the network can call them, so a single compromised component inherits the authority of every service it can route to.
risks.mitigation: Identify the edges that reach the highest-value data and add edge authorisation to those specifically, rather than deferring the whole pattern.

risks.statement: Point-to-point edge count grows combinatorially, and the integration test matrix grows with it - the schedule impact lands late, in test rather than build.
risks.mitigation: Cap the number of new point-to-point edges and route new consumers through a shared edge where one already exists.

risks.statement: Stubbed RTL interfaces mask real failure modes - timeouts, partial responses, throttling - so the first genuine test of those behaviours is in Prod.
risks.mitigation: Prioritise real sandbox connectivity for the interfaces on the critical path, and record the remainder as an accepted test gap.

lld_notes: Per interface: protocol, authN, authZ decision point, transport protection, payload protection, log emitted, and the trust boundary it crosses.
Mark every interface that is stubbed in RTL and state what behaviour the stub does not reproduce.
hld_notes: Trust boundaries must be drawn on the e2e flow; an edge with no marked boundary is an unexamined assumption.

options.name: Managed API gateway with verified authorisation at every trust-boundary edge
options.summary: Internal and external APIs route through a managed gateway carrying authentication, authorisation, rate limiting and per-edge logging. Authorisation is verified at the edge on every boundary crossing, never inferred from location.
checklist: every trust-boundary edge routed through a policy enforcement point
per-edge authN, authZ, transport and payload protection recorded
contract and schema governance with versioning and a deprecation policy
sync vs async decided per interface with idempotency and replay handling on async paths
third-party integrations registered with materiality assessment
per-interface logging sufficient for a detection to consume, not just for debugging
gateway present in RTL with the same policy set as Prod
gateway failure mode stated per edge

questions.question: Are there edges that bypass the gateway for performance or legacy reasons, and what authorises those?
Does every interface emit a log with enough context for a detection - subject, resource, outcome, correlation id?
Which third parties are material or critical under the applicable regime, and does each have an exit plan?
What is the gateway's own availability tier, given it is now on the critical path for every edge?

anchors.note: The bypass count is the honest measure of edge-authorisation coverage.

risks.statement: The gateway becomes a single point of failure for every integration, inheriting the strictest availability requirement of any edge it carries.
risks.mitigation: Size and tier the gateway to the strictest caller, deploy it multi-AZ, and define per-edge behaviour on gateway failure explicitly.

risks.statement: Edges permitted to bypass the gateway for latency or legacy reasons are exactly the edges with no enforced authorisation, and they accumulate.
risks.mitigation: Register every bypass with an owner and expiry, and place compensating detection on those paths specifically.

risks.statement: Onboarding existing interfaces to a gateway requires coordination with every consuming team, and the schedule depends on their availability rather than the programme's.
risks.mitigation: Sequence onboarding in waves negotiated with consumer teams up front, and run gateway and direct paths in parallel during cutover.

risks.statement: Per-edge logging at gateway granularity is a large and frequently unbudgeted SIEM ingestion cost.
risks.mitigation: Pin the per-edge log volume anchor and agree the Type 1/Type 2 split with SecOps before build.

lld_notes: Publish the interface register as the primary artefact: one row per edge with trust boundary, authN, authZ, transport, payload protection, classification and log.
State the gateway policy applied per edge and the failure mode if the gateway is unavailable.
Record every bypass with its justification, owner and expiry.
hld_notes: The gateway is the enforcement plane on the e2e flow; every boundary crossing passes through it, and the exceptions are drawn explicitly.

options.name: Event-driven backbone with schema governance and idempotent consumers
options.summary: Services integrate asynchronously over a governed event backbone. Schemas are registered and versioned, consumers are idempotent, and replay and poison-message handling are designed rather than discovered. Sits alongside a gateway for synchronous edges.
checklist: topic inventory with an owner, a classification and a retention position per topic
schema registry with compatibility policy and a stated deprecation path
consumer idempotency proven, not assumed - replay must be safe
poison-message and dead-letter handling defined per consumer group, with an owner for the queue
topic-level authorisation using workload identity rather than shared credentials
message-level classification recorded - a topic can carry a higher classification than its consumers hold
replay of retained events assessed as a data-exposure path in its own right
ordering and exactly-once expectations stated honestly per consumer

questions.question: Is every consumer genuinely idempotent, and has replay been tested rather than asserted?
Topic retention means the backbone is a data store - what classification does it hold, and is it protected to that level?
Who owns the dead-letter queue, and what is the agreed time before an un-actioned poison message becomes an incident?
Can a consumer with replay rights reconstruct a data set it is not authorised to query directly?

anchors.note: Retention makes the backbone a datastore; it belongs in the Data domain's store inventory.

risks.statement: Event retention turns the backbone into an unclassified datastore holding whatever the highest-classification topic carries, usually outside the Data domain's store inventory.
risks.mitigation: Register every topic in the datastore inventory with its classification and apply the same encryption, retention and access rules as any other store.

risks.statement: Replay rights let a consumer reconstruct history it could not query directly, which is an authorisation bypass expressed as a feature.
risks.mitigation: Authorise replay separately from consumption and log every replay as a Type 1 event.

risks.statement: Non-idempotent consumers turn any redelivery into duplicated business effect - duplicated payments, duplicated notifications - and redelivery is normal, not exceptional.
risks.mitigation: Test idempotency with deliberate redelivery in RTL as an acceptance gate, not as a non-functional aspiration.

risks.statement: Schema evolution across independently released consumers is a coordination cost that recurs every release, and it is rarely in the plan after go-live.
risks.mitigation: Fix the compatibility policy before the first topic is published and enforce it in the pipeline rather than in review.

lld_notes: Per topic: owner, schema, compatibility policy, classification, retention, consumers, and the authorisation model.
State the idempotency mechanism per consumer and the test that proves it.
Record dead-letter ownership and the escalation path.
hld_notes: The backbone is drawn as both an integration path and a datastore, because retention makes it both.

options.name: Governed third-party integration tier with exit and concentration management
options.summary: External and third-party integration is handled by a dedicated tier with materiality assessment, contractual control mapping, exit planning and concentration analysis. Selected where third parties carry material or critical dependency.
checklist: third-party register complete with materiality and CTP assessment per party
contractual right-to-audit, sub-outsourcing and incident-notification terms confirmed per material party
exit plan documented and costed per material party, with a stated exit execution time
concentration risk assessed across parties, including shared fourth parties
asynchronous paths to and from each party - callbacks, webhooks, file transfers - made idempotent, with replay and duplicate handling defined per party
data shared with each party classified, with the sharing agreement referenced
each party's own incident notification path tested, not just contracted
egress allow-list entries reconciled one to one against the third-party register

questions.question: Which third parties meet the critical-third-party threshold, and has that assessment been reviewed by compliance rather than assumed by architecture?
Do several material parties depend on the same fourth party, creating concentration the individual assessments do not show?
How long would exit actually take for the most material party, and does that fit the impact tolerance stated for the service?
Is there an egress allow-list entry with no corresponding entry in the third-party register?
For each party sending us asynchronous traffic, is a redelivery safe - and has that been tested rather than assumed?

risks.statement: An exit plan that exists on paper but has never been costed or rehearsed will not satisfy supervisory challenge, and the gap surfaces during a review rather than during design.
risks.mitigation: Cost each exit and rehearse the highest-materiality one at least in tabletop, recording the result as evidence.

risks.statement: Concentration through a shared fourth party is invisible in per-party assessments, so the aggregate dependency is larger than any individual record shows.
risks.mitigation: Map fourth-party dependencies explicitly and assess concentration at the portfolio level rather than per contract.

risks.statement: Contractual remediation with existing suppliers depends on their commercial cycle and can take longer than the technical delivery it gates.
risks.mitigation: Start contract remediation in parallel with design, not after it, and treat each renegotiation as a dated external dependency.

risks.statement: Third-party incident notification is often contractual rather than technical, so the first indication of a supplier breach may be an email days later.
risks.mitigation: Establish a technical notification path where possible and build detection for anomalous behaviour on the party's own integration.

lld_notes: Publish the third-party register with materiality, data shared, contractual position and exit time per party.
Reconcile the register against the Network egress allow-list; an unmatched entry on either side is a finding.
Record the fourth-party map alongside the party register.
hld_notes: Third parties appear on the e2e flow as named external boundaries with their materiality marked, not as anonymous clouds.
